question.en:
Select the most appropriate sentence to complete the given paragraph.

Many public libraries in small towns have begun lending e-books through mobile apps. Readers who once had to travel long distances can now borrow a title within minutes. Librarians report that young readers, in particular, are returning in large numbers. ________

solution_text.en:
Find the thread.

• Libraries now lend e-books by app.

• Readers no longer need to travel.

• Young readers are returning.

The closing line should draw the lesson from this: going digital brings readers back.

Option does exactly that: meeting them where they already are (on their phones) → win back their lost readers.

Why the others are wrong.

• Remove printed books: an extreme conclusion; nothing in the paragraph criticises printed books or says young readers reject them.

• Mobile phones harm eyesight: changes the topic to health, and 'however' sets up a contrast the paragraph never builds.

• Fewer schools and colleges: an unrelated fact about small towns.

Answer: The trend suggests that libraries can win back their lost readers simply by meeting them where they already are.

A good concluding line sums up the paragraph; it does not jump to an extreme or a new topic.

solution_text.en:
The passage begins with the survey's figures and ends with its demand:

"What the survey points to is the need for planning that treats transport and housing as two halves of the same problem."

"The survey has done its job by supplying the evidence; it is now for planners to turn it into action."

So the title must carry both the data and the joint planning of transport and housing.

Why the others are wrong.

• Long commutes must be cut: the passage calls the 25-minute average "relatively short". The problem is cost and poor public transport, not commute length.

• End urban pollution: pollution is one side effect mentioned in the second paragraph; the passage never claims transport reform will end it.

• Low-cost housing: the answer: housing is only "the other half of the solution". This title drops transport, the main subject.

Answer: Commuting Data That Calls for Joined-Up Planning

Word help.

• unflattering (जो अच्छी छवि न दिखाए)

• woefully inadequate (बेहद अपर्याप्त)

• joined-up (आपस में जुड़ा, समन्वित)

A title that holds only half of the solution is the commonest trap in title questions.

solution_text.en:
"…ringed by slums, not because anyone planned it that way but because workers cannot afford to live far from their jobs when getting there is costly and slow."

Travel is expensive and slow → workers settle near their jobs, even in slums.

Why the others are wrong.

• Deliberately set up by authorities: the passage says "not because anyone planned it that way".

• Free housing from factory owners: never mentioned.

• Cleaner air: the passage says the opposite; pollution is "choking these same cities".

Answer: Costly and slow commuting pushes workers to live as near their places of work as they can

solution_text.en:
"These are foundations to build on, not grounds for complacency."

The short commute and the suburban railways are good points, but the author warns against feeling so pleased with them that nothing more is done.

Complacency = a feeling of being satisfied with oneself, so that one stops trying to improve (आत्मसंतोष, आत्मतुष्टि).

Smugness = the same self-satisfied feeling (आत्मतुष्टि, अपने पर इतराना).

Why the others are wrong.

• Vigilance = staying alert and watchful for problems (सतर्कता): opposite meaning — the trap. The author wants vigilance, not complacency.

• Arrogance = feeling superior to others (अहंकार): same field (too much self-regard), but it is about looking down on others, not resting on one's success.

• Compliance = obeying a rule or request (अनुपालन): look-alike of complacency, unrelated meaning.

Answer: Smugness

Word help.

• foundations (नींव, आधार)

'Not grounds for complacency' = don't relax just because a few things are going well.

solution_text.en:
The author's claim:

"A safe, radial network… will help little if the homes along it are priced beyond the reach of those who most need it. Housing that is genuinely low-cost, placed where the network runs, is the other half of the solution."

Option gives evidence that housing + transport together worked: more people used transit and saved money. It directly supports the claim.

Why the others are wrong.

• Workers prefer two-wheelers anyway: suggests transit would not be used even if provided, which weakens the case.

• Commuting costs have fallen with no change in housing: undercuts the problem the author describes and suggests transport alone can fix it, so it weakens the argument.

• Metro through expensive areas still used by low-wage workers: shows transit works without low-cost housing nearby, which weakens the need for joint planning.

Answer: Where low-cost housing was built along new bus and train routes, both ridership and workers' savings rose sharply.

Word help.

• ridership (सवारियों की संख्या)

• genuinely (वास्तव में, सचमुच)

option_2.en: Riya said that if I had a car, I would drive to work.

option_3.en: Riya said that if she had a car, she would drive to work.

option_4.en: Riya said that if she has a car, she will drive to work.

question.en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.

Riya said, "If I had a car, I would drive to work."

solution_text.en:
Rule: In indirect speech, unreal conditionals (second and third) keep their verb forms; there is no backshift. Only a first conditional (will) changes will → would. Pronouns change as usual.

Example: He said, "If I were rich, I would help the poor." → He said that if he were rich, he would help the poor.

(काल्पनिक शर्त वाले वाक्य का काल नहीं बदलता)

Apply it.

"If I had a car, I would drive" is a second conditional (an unreal present idea).

• Tenses stay: had… would drive

• Pronouns change: I → she

→ Riya said that if she had a car, she would drive to work.

Why the others are wrong.

• had had… would have driven: wrongly backshifted; this turns it into a third conditional (a past regret) and changes the meaning.

• if I had… I would drive: pronouns not changed.

• if she has… she will drive: moves the verbs forward, which is never done in reported speech; it also makes the idea sound real.

Answer: Riya said that if she had a car, she would drive to work.

Second and third conditionals: change the pronouns, leave the tenses alone.

option_1.en: It was said that the old fort has a secret tunnel.

option_2.en: It is said that the old fort has a secret tunnel.

option_3.en: It is being said that the old fort has a secret tunnel.

option_4.en: The old fort is said that it has a secret tunnel.

question.en:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

People say that the old fort has a secret tunnel.

solution_text.en:
Rule: 'People / They say that + clause' becomes It is said that + clause. 'People' is a general agent, so 'by people' is dropped. The tense of say is kept: say → is said, said → was said. The that-clause stays unchanged.

Example: People say that he is honest. → It is said that he is honest.

(अवैयक्तिक कर्मवाच्य)

Apply it.

• People say (simple present) → It is said

• that the old fort has a secret tunnel → unchanged

→ It is said that the old fort has a secret tunnel.

Why the others are wrong.

• It was said: changes simple present to simple past.

• It is being said: changes simple present to present continuous.

• The old fort is said that it has…: mixes two patterns. With the fort as subject the correct form is The old fort is said to have a secret tunnel; 'is said that' cannot follow a noun subject.

Answer: It is said that the old fort has a secret tunnel.

'People say that' → 'It is said that': keep the tense of 'say', keep the clause.

question.en:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

My father chose this scooter because it is very ________ on fuel.

solution_text.en:
Meaning: economical = using little of something, such as fuel or money; giving good value (किफ़ायती, कम खर्च वाला)

economical on fuel is a fixed collocation: the scooter uses little petrol.

Why the others are wrong.

• economic = related to the economy or trade (आर्थिक), as in economic growth. It is not used with 'on fuel'.

• economics = the subject that studies production and wealth (अर्थशास्त्र): a noun.

• economy = the system of trade of a country, or careful use of money (अर्थव्यवस्था; बचत): a noun; very economy is impossible.

Answer: economical

Economic = of the economy; economical = saves fuel or money.

question.en:
Arrange the following sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A. At first, his pots cracked in the kiln, and he nearly gave up.

B. Raghav learned pottery from his grandmother when he was twelve.

C. Today, his bowls are sold in craft shops across three states.

D. But she taught him to dry the clay slowly, and the cracks soon disappeared.

solution_text.en:
Opener test.

B names the person (Raghav) and the teacher (his grandmother). A begins with 'his', D with 'But she', C with 'Today, his'; all need an earlier noun. So B opens.

Links.

• B → A: "At first" begins the story of his learning; 'his pots' = Raghav's pots.

• A → D: "But she": 'she' = the grandmother; 'But' contrasts with he nearly gave up; the cracks picks up cracked in A.

• D → C: "Today" jumps to the present result, so C closes.

The paragraph.

Raghav learned pottery from his grandmother when he was twelve. At first, his pots cracked in the kiln, and he nearly gave up. But she taught him to dry the clay slowly, and the cracks soon disappeared. Today, his bowls are sold in craft shops across three states.

Time words (at first → today) and pronouns (she = grandmother) fix the chain.

Word help: kiln (भट्ठी जिसमें मिट्टी के बर्तन पकाए जाते हैं)
